turns.learner: Yesterday I go to the market and I buy many fruits.
turns.correction: I went to the market and I bought many fruits.
turns.shortExample: Yesterday I went to the market.
turns.beginnerReply: Nice trip! What fruit did you buy?
turns.intermediateReply: That sounds nice, and I wonder which fruit you ended up buying?
turns.advancedReply: Interesting. Setting aside the tense slips, what made you choose the market over the supermarket?

turns.learner: The fruits was very expensive but I buy two kilos of apples.
turns.correction: The fruits were very expensive, so I bought two kilos of apples.
turns.shortExample: The apples were expensive, so I bought two kilos.
turns.intermediateReply: Good choice, although I would have bought fewer apples if the price was that high.
turns.advancedReply: Fair enough, though I would have negotiated the price or waited for a cheaper stall.

turns.learner: Yesterday I explain the project to my team and everyone agree with the plan.
turns.correction: Yesterday I explained the project to my team and everyone agreed with the plan.
turns.shortExample: Yesterday I explained the plan to my team.
turns.intermediateReply: That is good news, and since everyone agreed, I wonder what the next step will be.
turns.advancedReply: A rare consensus, surely. Did anyone challenge the timeline, or did the plan sail through untouched?

turns.learner: We was discussing the budget when the manager arrives late to the meeting.
turns.correction: We were discussing the budget when the manager arrived late to the meeting.
turns.shortExample: We were discussing the budget when he arrived.
turns.beginnerReply: Oh no! The meeting started late.
turns.intermediateReply: That sounds awkward, although late arrivals are common when meetings overlap.
turns.advancedReply: Unfortunate, yet predictable: recurring overruns say more about the calendar than about the manager.
